168	- **Questions for him:** section 9's list.
169	
170	## 9. For Pavol
171	
172	**What you asked.** On 26 October you wrote that you doubted whether the decisions the revival rests on were good and well informed, or a mistake. You named the bound as a possible linchpin, and you asked that the three layers be kept apart: what the Fortress language says; how the team built it on the Java virtual machine; and how Fortress meets Java.
173	
174	**The verdict, first.**
175	
176	- None of the nine foundational decisions was a mistake. All nine hold.
177	- Three of them were taken on information that was incomplete or partly wrong. In every case, the missing or corrected fact makes your decision stronger or leaves it as it is. None weakens it.
178	- The layers were mixed in the reasons written under your decisions, not in the decisions. Four entries give a reason from the wrong layer, or call a 2009 piece of code "later" than a 2011 paper. The rewrites fix the reasons. No decision turns.
179	
180	**The bound, in plain words.** A type parameter is a placeholder for a type, like the `T` in `List[\T\]`. Its bound is the largest type the placeholder may stand for. `Any` is the type of every value. `Object` is the type of every value except tuples (pairs such as `(3, 4)`), functions, and the empty value `()`. You decided that a placeholder with no written bound means `Any`.
181	
182	- The language, layer one, says `Any`. The team's last paper, from 2019, with Steele and Ryu among its authors, says in so many words that the default bound is `Any`. The team's library, which is their statement of the language's library, writes its placeholders without a bound and fills them with tuples. The 2011 draft's sentence saying `Object` is not in the 2008 text, appears in 2009 in a list of "Not Yet Implemented Features", and sits beside a sentence in the same section saying placeholders take tuple types, which `Object` would forbid.
183	- The team's build on the virtual machine, layer two, does not need `Object`. In May 2012 Steele implemented the draft's sentence on the compiled path, saying it was "amazingly" not yet implemented. The next day it broke the interpreter's tests. He did not change the interpreter or the library. He made the sentence a setting that is on for the compiled path and off for the interpreter, and he wrote `Any` by hand in every compiled library and test that needed tuples. That is enforcing a sentence on one path, not choosing the language's rule. No team text says the compiled path needs `Object`. A probe this week turned the setting off: tuples and functions as type arguments compile and run exactly as they do today when `Any` is written. With the setting on, as the compile command has it today, a call `id((3, 4))` compiles and silently runs `id(3)`.
184	- Java, layer three, maps its own `Object` type to Fortress `Any`, not to Fortress `Object`. Nothing in the record ever used Java as a reason for the bound.
185	- What you were told on 29 September had two errors: that "nothing in the code changes" (one line in `Shell.java` does), and that the 2012 Types chapter puts functions outside `Object` (it puts them inside; tuples stay outside). You were not told that Steele turned the setting on for the compiled path on purpose. Your yes rested on the tuples, and the tuples decide it. The decision stands.
186	- The bound is not a linchpin. Only one line of code and ten test files rest on it.
187	
188	**The compiler's small library, in plain words.** The team built two libraries: the interpreter's full one, and a small one for the compiler that they called "bogus", a "bogo-trait" and a "hopefully temporary hack". You decided the full one is the one library, and you asked whether we ported the small library's good designs back or just taught the checker to accept whatever the full library said.
189	
190	- Both happened, and the sweep finds the choice was weighed every time the two differed on a design. Taken from the small library: the flat number types, the numeral type, ranges over 32-bit integers, each integer type's own `MIN` and `MAX`, the integer power, lazy comparison, and the rule that a component declares every member its interface marks abstract. Weighed and not taken, with the reason now dated: the small library's `fail` returning a declared bottom type (Steele, June 2011), which the team's own 2012 and 2019 texts later made unwritable; the small library's `comprises T` spelling of the self type (Steele, June 2012), whose fact the checker now reads from the bound, as Naden's last note pointed; and string concatenation with the string on the left only, which the specification's own rule contradicts.
191	- The rule for the future, which goes into the record: a design of the small library binds the full one when the team's later word on the language backs it, or when the team's text is unclear and the team's own checker enforced the design as a rule. A stub by the team's own words does not bind. "Later" is a date: a 2009 line of code is not later than a 2011 paper.
192	- One place we had the full library's text against a backed design of the small one: the abstract members (row 816). You reversed that on 25 October. The sweep finds no other.
193	
194	**The decisions to take, each with a default.**
195	
196	1. **Close phase 3 with climb batch 22c.** Phase 3 is the work that made the type checker accept the full library's twelve core parts without error. Your framing is sound. The batch carries four rungs: the abstract-member repair you decided; the nine operator headers that differ between interface and component, with the export check made to read operators; the two library parts that `List` imports and the count never checked; and the one line that gives the compile command the `Any` bound, with ten test edits. The batch's exit: the checker reports no error over those thirteen parts, under the compile command's own setting. Everything that is about generating or running code stays in phase 4. Default: yes.
197	2. **Confirm that the 40 other library parts do not block the switch-over.** They hold 624 errors. They block the later step where the interpreter runs the checker on its own programs. Each is cleared before that step, or before the first program that needs it. Default: yes.
198	3. **Rewrite the reasons under five entries, through the trap test you approved.** The entries: the team's later word (P-26), one library (P-37), the flat numbers (P-43), the bound (P-42), the phases (P-33), and smaller corrections to five more. The new texts must make the coordinator weigh in the right layer and date "later" correctly. You said yes to this on 26 October. Default: proceed; nothing enters until a trap test passes.
199	4. **Three one-word answers, each in your own entry.** Drop "functions" from the bound's entry, since the team's texts disagree on functions and agree on tuples. Default: drop. Strike the sentence "The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text" from P-26; the coordinator added it with no source. Default: strike. Move the two sentences of P-43's "Why" to history and write the language's grounds in their place. Default: yes.
200	5. **Say yes, informed, to the natives' form before batch 23.** A native is a library function whose body is Java. The decision keeps the library's own form, `builtinPrimitive("...")`, and changes only the string, to name a static Java method both paths can call. The language has no rule here, so the library's practice decides. After the 449 bindings move, the other form costs a library sweep. Default: yes, as decided.
201	6. **One lean to confirm, no decision yet.** On 20 September you leaned to the class loader as the way to store a vector of doubles as a Java `double[]`. The lean was never recorded. Record it as a lean under the array decisions, to be measured; stamping a class per type, which the loader does today, gives no `double[]` field by itself. Default: record as a lean.
202	
203	**Two things to know, no decision needed.** The probe found a compiled-path defect that does not depend on the bound: a generic method with one tuple-typed parameter dies at the call. It gets a ledger row. And the small library's cast failure is an unchecked exception where the full library's is checked; this matters only when the checker starts checking `throws` clauses, and it will come to you then.

3	# The phase 3 exit and the foundations review: the dialogue
4	
5	All times UTC; his time was UTC+2 until 01:00 UTC on 10-25 and UTC+1 after. His messages are quoted in the session transcript `fe616d40-…jsonl` at the times given. This file holds what was understood and agreed; POSITIONS holds only what he decided, and the boot note what is in flight.
6	
7	## 1. How he wants things explained (applies to every later answer)
8	
9	- **Precision first.** At 04:53:38 on 10-26 he refused to go on because one sentence of mine was false ("the numbered POSITIONS, which started on 10-13": POSITIONS began on 2026-09-15, `8ab10d9de`; the numbering came on 10-13; the library route entered POSITIONS at 02:36 on 09-21, `581a29510`, restored at 02:40, `3e85b709c`). Check every factual sentence against git or the record before writing it.
10	- **Read in full before answering from a note.** At 04:59:24 he refused to engage while I worked from condensed parts of three notes. Name what I read and how much; read a note whole before I summarise it to him.
11	- **A logical argument, not clues.** At 19:35:13 on 10-25: give the status quo, the library's way, and the current solution, in order, as an argument. Not the nine steps in full, but their spine.
12	- **ASD-STE100 register; no self-flagellation** (19:27:02). State the cause and the fix; do not apologise at length.
13	- **Keep the three layers apart** (his frame, 05:25:27 on 10-26): what Fortress the language says; how the team implemented it on the JVM; how Fortress meets Java. A ground in one layer does not decide a question in another. I had let the library-route judgement of 09-20 read a sentence of the Working Draft (layer 1) as the reason for a compiled-path setting (layer 2).
14	- **POSITIONS is mainly for the coordinator** (07:48:49): for my judgement after compactions and restarts, when I plan a batch or a probe, so that I orient the work right. Its entries must resolve contradictions with enough context that I know how to weigh trade-offs. Rewrites are done very carefully.
15	- **Don't over-engineer**, but test what matters (07:42:15, 07:54:36).
16	
17	## 2. The skipped boot (10-25, 18:50 to 19:20)
18	
19	- After the compaction of 10-24 I did not boot: the summary's "resume directly" and a worker's hand-back at the turn's top pulled me past the hook. He asked why (18:50:58). No good reason.
20	- At his word (19:06:08: "if there is a minimal change, you can do it") I added a boot check to the model-check Stop hook (`.claude/hooks/model-check.sh`, `05a4fdb11`): after the transcript's last compaction, both skills must have been loaded with the Skill tool, or the stop is blocked once with a reminder. Replayed on the transcript at 16:33 on 10-24 it fires; now it passes. It runs at every turn's end and acts only on the first turn after a compaction.
21	
22	## 3. Row 816 and P-158 (10-25 19:06 to 10-26 04:28)
23	
24	**The argument, in the order he asked for it (19:35:13):**
25	
26	1. *The two paths call a method differently.* Walk finds a method on the object by name at the call; the trait need not declare it. The compiled path calls through the trait's Java interface; if the trait does not declare the method, the call dies with `NoSuchMethodError`.
27	2. *The team's two libraries each followed their path.* The compiler's prelude: the api writes `abstract loop(body: ZZ32->()): ()` in `GeneratorZZ32`; the component restates `loop(body: ZZ32->()): ()` with no body; the objects give the body (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi:112-120`, `.fss:301-312`). The team's export check enforced it (its count written by Sukyoung Ryu, `ac0d41de0`, 2009-05-08; first written here as Chase's of 2012, `5a68404fd`, a parentless snapshot): a component trait with fewer members than its api trait is refused. The interpreter's library, written for walk and never compiled by the team, sometimes leaves an api's `abstract` member out of the component's trait (`String`'s `split`), and walk does not care.
28	3. *What the revival changed.* When the checker read the interpreter's library, the team's check refused 12 such members. Two ways: (a) add the 12 declarations to the components, the compiled library's way; (b) weaken the check. Climb batch 21b's rung E took (b) (`031c38bbc`), from a misreading of `apis.tex` ("includes definitions for all declarations other than … abstract" read as "needs no member", where it says "needs no body"). The chain: an Opus ways worker of 10-20 (`reviews/array-sites-ways.md`, "4i", "Decision: none, since it is the text's own rule"); the export probe of 10-23 built it; batch 21's planner made it fork 20 with the default "the team's own text"; its Fable review and I passed it as not consequential; rung E built it; its skeptic found the `NoSuchMethodError` after the build; the 21b review kept it as "it cannot happen yet"; batch 22 carried it as question 1 and I launched batch 22 at about 02:01 on 10-24 without sending him the question. No document before the change mentions `NoSuchMethodError`. Root cause: one sentence misread; nobody read the code it changed (the team's deliberate count) or asked what a compiled call does; the change cleared errors, which was the batch's goal.
29	4. *The fix (his option 2).* Restore the team's count; add 12 bodyless declarations to five component traits (`String` 7: `depth`, `isBalanced`, `verify`, `rangeContains`, `balanced`, `splitWithOffsets`, `split`; `Range`'s `isEmpty`; `ReadableArray`'s `opr[_:TrivialOpenRange]`; `ActualReduction`'s `empty` and `join`; `AnyMaybe`'s `holds`). No body, not an empty body: an empty body makes the method concrete, and then no object must define it.
30	
31	**His decision:** option 2 (19:06:08 on 10-25); his reason (04:28:41 on 10-26): "by the standing position that later team's work supersedes earlier one, we take the compiled path's way over the walk library's. That's why 21b should have chosen (a), not weaken the check — we must reverse this." Recorded as P-158 (`edbd0d4f5`, reason `5da8144e4`); F-282 and row 816 rewritten; PLAN's phase 4 line "Row 816's repair". At 07:30:36 he placed the repair in climb batch 22c (section 6).
32	
33	## 4. The library route and its premise (10-26, 04:31 to 05:25)
34	
35	- Ask 2 (is phase 3 done, its exit restated) led to his statement of the goal (04:47:50): "The whole point of the switch-over is to avoid the need to port walk's library into the compiler's library. The revival is continuing the development of the type checker, so that it would accept the fuller Fortress library that the interpreter uses." P-37 lacks this reason; it goes in with the rewrites (section 8).
36	- The history, read in full at his insistence (`postmortem-2026-09-19/direction-history-transcripts.md`, `two-libraries.md`, `library-route-judgement.md`): on 09-15 he did not know there were two libraries; at 23:51 on 09-15 he asked "Couldn't the path forward be just to use the FortressLibrary for compiler as well?"; a probe (00:13 on 09-16) found 95% of the library plain Fortress, but desugaring and code generation were never reached; the coordinator put the fork twice as "not needed yet" (09-16) and on 09-17 chose the porting route for him, unpriced, and he accepted an order of steps; on 09-20 the post-mortem found this; his words "we need to unify this. into single library", "the compiler second library is just a bootstrap and we need to get rid of it" (P-37). Maessen's 2008 comment calls the switch a "hopefully temporary hack as we work on importing java objects cleanly" (its reason Java imports, not the checker); the team left no plan to end the split and grew the prelude until June 2012; the specification knows one library.
37	- **The other 40 components** (624 errors, 25 crashes, F-290) are outside phase 3's twelve. He agreed the plan never meant them for phase 3 ("Of course"), but the goal is the fuller library. My view, his to confirm: they do not block the switch-over; they block P-12's step (walk runs the checker), so each reaches zero before that step or before the first program that needs it.
38	- At 05:25:27 he doubted the premise ("whether I made a good and well informed decision, or a mistake"), named the bound as a possible linchpin, and asked to re-verify the foundational tenets: the foundations review (section 5).
39	
40	## 5. The foundations review (approved 06:11:21)
41	
42	**Scope, nine tenets, each ground filed by the three layers:** 1 the goal (P-7, P-8); 2 the team's later word (P-26); 3 one library (P-37), premise that the compiled path can run it, not only check it; 4 the bound `Any` (P-42); 5 the exclusion rule and flat numbers (P-43); 6 the phase order (P-33); 7 unboxed doubles and `double[]` (P-17, P-84); 8 the natives' form (P-58); 9 walk runs the checker (P-12, P-59).
43	
44	**Step 1, done.**
45	- `reviews/foundations/bound-archaeology.md` (`ab2ee0c29`): the Working Draft's `Object` sentence is not in 1.0 (2008), first in bulk imports of 2009-11; later team texts split (Welterweight, the 2011 paper, POPL 2019 p. 11:9 give `Any`; Naden 2012 calls `Object` "the distinguished top type"; a 2008 commit left "either Object or Any" open). Steele wrote the compiled path's `Object` default on 2012-05-28 (`91e71e62e`, "amazingly, this was not yet implemented", writing `extends Any` into the compiled libraries and tests that take tuples, arrows or `()`), turned it off on 05-29 "so that interpreter tests will pass" (`c61723f61`), and made it a setting, on for the compiled path, on 05-30 (`afb02f41d`). No team text says the compiled path needs `Object`. `java.lang.Object` maps to Fortress `Any` (`NamingCzar.java:447`). On 09-29 he was told the compiled path writes `Object` and that Steele switched it off for the interpreter tests, but not that Steele switched it on for the compiled path as the language's rule; two statements of mine that day were wrong (the sentence's date; "the Types chapter has `Object` exclude function types").
46	- `perf-probes/bound-any-compiled/REPORT.md` (`4b3d91cb4`): under `Any`, tuple and arrow static arguments compile, load and run (same classes and bytecode as with `extends Any` written); `()` dies with `AbstractMethodError` under both bounds (row 339); a new defect: a generic dotted method with one tuple-typed parameter dies with `ClassCastException` (`CodeGen.java:6250-6263`), both bounds, no row yet; under `Object`, `id((3, 4))` compiles as `id(3)` (row 691); `ant testQuick` under `Any`: 12 failures in 10 compiler tests, all test-side; the switch is one small rung. Its findings for the ledger and FACTS, and its two questions (when `Any` reaches `fortress compile`; `CoercionGenericFnCompiledRungC`), wait for the judgement.
47	
48	**Step 2, done.** `reviews/foundations/tenets-evidence.md` (`6c6437dfc`), read in full. Its new finds: the team's JVM type mapping relies on the exclusion rule (`Papers/Implementation/TypeMapping.tex:125`); the prelude's flattening of 2009 (`6896886fb`) is a code-generator commit with no stated reason; P-26's list of the later word counts layer-2 code (the prelude's flattening, the export check, the powers) as the language's word; "specialization kept" names a layer-1 thing in P-26 and a layer-2 thing in `exploring.md:20`; walk cannot run the checker as set (Scala off, the Java checker gone, no case for `CoercionInvocation`), so P-12's "small change" is not small; his class-loader lean of 09-20 for the unboxed store was never recorded; he was told on 09-19 that stamping "only renames" (no generic instance holds a `double[]`) and on 09-24 that "unboxing will build on it"; his informed yes to P-58 is still owed. Its tensions: P-37's ruling called the prelude "what they could do behind the JVM wall" (layer 2) while P-43's "Why" calls it "the team's last record of the Fortress way" (layer 1).
49	
50	**The prelude-lens sweep, running** (his yes 07:36:39; `reviews/foundations/prelude-lens.md` when it returns). His worry (07:30:36): where the two libraries differed, did we port the compiler prelude's legitimate later designs into the one library (as the flat numbers), or just extend the checker to accept whatever the interpreter library wrote? No review had swept for it: the phase 3 audit's Part B judged library changes against the interpreter library's own text and the specification and left the prelude out; no review compared checker changes with the prelude's way. Caution: the prelude was "stripped-down minimalist … for first crack at compilation", with parts the team called "bogus" and a "bogo-trait": the sweep sorts each prelude choice into a deliberate design (commit, author, date) or a bootstrap stub. Places we took the prelude's design: P-43, P-76, P-77, P-47; one where we did the opposite: row 816.
51	
52	**Step 3, next:** the Fable judgement on step 1, step 2 and the sweep (his go of 06:11:21 includes it), then a page for him by an Opus writer. Its brief must name the exclusion-fork notes directly (section 7).
53	
54	## 6. His framing of the phase (07:30:36)
55	
56	This is the phase 3 exit review. So far the tenets hold. If the judgement holds them, no major re-evaluation of direction is needed; phase 3 closes with one more batch, **climb batch 22c** (or more if needed), for the rungs left, to exit phase 3 cleanly. Candidates: row 816's repair (P-158); the 9 operator headers that differ between api and component (row 782); `List`'s two unchecked imports (`CovariantCollection`, `OneShotFlag`); the bound `Any` for `fortress compile` (the probe's one small rung). Batch 23 (the natives) follows. This takes the place of ask 2's options (phase 3 done with its exit restated, or open until the wider zero); P-33's phase 3 text is rewritten after the judgement. The earlier asks 3 to 8 (P-58's informed yes; P-155 to cover the export check; P-75 withdrawn; his texts to correct; rq 35 and rq 230; batch 23's go) are still open, after the review.
57	
58	## 7. The flat numbers: my framing corrected (07:46:17)
59	
60	I had framed the judge's question as whether the prelude's flat numbers are a design of the language or a JVM measure. He corrected me: the record's digging decided the flat tower, and I was wrong. The grounds on record: the exclusion rule in the team's language texts (the 2011 paper, `exclusion.tick:141-152`; the 2012 Types chapter, `types.tick:355-376`; Naden 2012, "blanket … for the semantic benefits and the simplicity"; POPL 2019 keeps it); under the rule a nested tower is impossible (`ZZ32 extends ZZ64`, both `Integral` at different arguments); the Working Draft says the number types "are mutually exclusive" (`types-vals-vars.tex:502`); Steele's 2016 talk shows a flat tower; the checker relies on the rule (F-44) and so does the JVM mapping (`TypeMapping.tex:125`); routes A, B and C weighed 09-22 to 09-24 (`reviews/multiple-instantiation-exclusion.md`, `reviews/exclusion-design-brief.md`, `reviews/mie-probes/`), A chosen 09-24; reviews D4 (09-29), the POPL recheck and V5 (10-23) keep it. What is open is narrower: P-43's stated reason, "the flattened prelude is the team's last record of the Fortress way", is the weakest ground and not his words (rq 219). The judge's real question for P-37: when does a design of the compiler's prelude bind the one library? My answer, for the judge to weigh: when the team's later word on the language backs it, as the exclusion rule backs the flat numbers.

This decision does not stop work on the code generator, which is compiler work under either library. The decision is not put to him again. 496	
497	> - P-17 **Unboxed doubles and arrays of unboxed doubles are required: without them the revival misses its point.** Why: a language meant for high performance cannot box its numbers. Today the code generator boxes every number: an `RR64` value is an object of the class `FRR64`. In Java models of microGPT's three array kernels, the dot product, the matrix product and the row lift, boxing is the main cost (F-11 holds the measurement). How arrays store doubles, as `double[]`, is P-84's decision.

499	POS.md:92:
500

624	## Tenet 9. Walk runs the checker after the switch-over (P-12, with P-59)
625	
626	### (a) The entries
627	
628	POS.md:12:
629	
630	> - P-12 **After the switch-over, walk runs the compiled type checker on its programs, and then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts.** The curator wants the checker usable on the programs that walk runs. Today `fortress typecheck` checks a program only against the compiler's prelude, so it is no check of walk's programs (F-9 holds this fact). Walk is not changed for this before the switch-over. After it, walk runs the checker on its programs and so gains their static types. Walk then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts, in place of its choice on the run-time value (P-59, walk's choice of coercions until the switch-over).
631	
632	POS.md:56:
633	
634	> - P-59 **Walk chooses a coercion by the run-time value until it runs the checker, after the switch-over.** Walk has no static types. So where a coercion is needed, walk chooses it by the value's run-time type. The specification and the compiled path choose it by the static type. The curator accepts this as the interpreter's limit, and walk is not changed for it before the switch-over. A callout in the coercion chapter (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex`) states the limit. Two expected-failure tests record it: `XXXCoercionStaticRungC`, the chapter's own printed example, and `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC`. After the switch-over, once walk runs the checker on its programs (P-12 orders the two steps), it uses the static coercions that the checker inserts. MicroGPT's static types are concrete, each the type of the value itself and not a trait above it, so on microGPT walk's choice and the static choice agree.

178	### 2.5 How the compiled run time represents `Any`, `Object`, tuples, arrows and `()`
179	
180	- **`Any`** is the JVM interface `fortress/AnyType$Any`: `TypeMapping.tex:87-89` ("the root of the Fortress type hierarchy and supertype of Tuples, Arrows, and Object"; first in `4a839480f`, David Chase, 2012-05-21); `NamingCzar.java:138-140`, `:225`; `runtimeSystem/Naming.java:137` (`ANY_TYPE_CLASS`), `:143` (`RTTI_GETTER_CLASS = ANY_TYPE_CLASS`). The Fortress source is `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fsi:14` `trait Any end` (first in `f5e78afde`, jmaessen, 2008-04-15). Every runtime value class extends `FValue`, `public abstract class FValue implements fortress.AnyType.Any` (`compiler/runtimeValues/FValue.java:14`), which declares `getRTTI()`. The class loader's generated `isA` methods test `instanceof fortress/AnyType$Any` and call `getRTTI` through it (`InstantiatingClassloader.java:1286-1330`).
181	- **`Object`** is a separate trait, `trait Object extends Any` (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:17`, `CompilerBuiltin.fss:354`, first in `c8d301411`, jmaessen, 2008-12-19; interpreter side `FortressBuiltin.fsi:32`, `2e3e67f18`). It declares the getters `asString`, `asExprString`, `asDebugString` (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:18-20`; `CompilerBuiltin.fss:355-357`); `Any` has no member (`AnyType.fsi:14`). It compiles to the interface `fortress/CompilerBuiltin$Object` (`TypeMapping.tex:84-85`: "the root for the Fortress trait hierarchy"). It is not `java/lang/Object`: `NamingCzar.java:170` `internalObject` is `Type.getInternalName(Object.class)`, used as the superclass of generated types (`CodeGen.java:5085-5087`).
182	- **Tuples**: interface `Tuple[\T1..Tn\]` with a super-interface `AnyTuple[\N\]` that extends `AnyType$Any`; the classes are generated by the loader (`InstantiatingClassloader.java:1676-1690`, `:2046-2074`; `TypeMapping.tex:141-154`, `:207-210`). Elements are read as `Any` (`FortressEncodings.tex:301-309` at `5c13fce7e`, dr2chase, 2011-01-29: `o1`..`oN` "returning `Fortress$AnyType$Any`"). `TupleRTTI.runtimeSupertypeOf` (`TupleRTTI.java:28-41`) is the Java test or an element-wise test of the same arity. `TypeMapping.tex:154`: tuple subtype queries "are compiled into element-by-element subtype queries". `:151` states the covariance with `Object` as the element top ("if X, Y, and Z each extend Object, then (X,Y,Z) extends (Object,Y,Z), ..."), and `:196` speaks of the subtyping between `(T,U,V)` and `(Object, Object, Object)` that "might be compiled ahead of time".
183	- **Arrows**: interface `Arrow[\dom..., range\]` with up to three `apply` methods (`TypeMapping.tex:156-167`; `InstantiatingClassloader.java:942-1000`, `:1185-1260`). `ArrowRTTI.runtimeSupertypeOf` (`ArrowRTTI.java:43-57`) is contravariant in inputs and covariant in the output. `TypeMapping.tex:167`: the third `apply` "receives the argument list as a single Tuple of the appropriate element types; this is necessary to support certain forms of generic instantiation (if a type parameter is instantiated with a Tuple, for example)".
184	- **`()`**: the value is `FVoid` (`compiler/runtimeValues/FVoid.java:14`, `extends FValue`, so it implements `AnyType.Any`); its RTTI is `VoidRTTI`, whose `runtimeSupertypeOf` answers true only for another `VoidRTTI` (`VoidRTTI.java:13-16`; "Fixed glitch with RTTI of void", David Chase, `a9c625b1e`, 2012-06-19); in generated names it is the snowman `☃` (`Naming.java:175`, `:305`; `TypeMapping.tex:107`, "`()` as a static parameter").
185	- **`Bottom`** is erased to `java/lang/Object` (`NamingCzar.java:206`, `81d727ad8`, David Chase, 2012-06-18, "Some cleanup related to bottom types name conversion and modeling in the JVM"; `:1297-1306`).
186	- **Generic classes** are template classes instantiated by the loader with RTTI objects as static arguments (`TypeMapping.tex:114-125`, `MethodMapping.tex:98-120`); `NamingCzar.forVarType` leaves a naked type variable as its name (`NamingCzar.java:1427-1431`), which the loader replaces at instantiation. The team's notes on the cost: `MethodMapping.tex:435`, "Covariant generics with Any-bounded static parameters (for example AnyList[\ T extends Any \]) will create special headaches because Tuple and Arrow type relationions are far too large to encode into the Java type system. One possibility will simply be to forbid that case; otherwise, it can be implemented by wrapping values ..." (the same sentence is in `FortressEncodings.tex` since `5c13fce7e`, 2011-01-29). `MethodMapping.tex:430`: "Each Fortress Object (perhaps not Any, meaning not Tuples, not Arrows) will have a method getRTTI()" (first in `c45132992`, David Chase, 2011-03-29).

The revival revises the specification to reconcile contradictions: where the team's later work, in the compiler or in the papers on types, contradicts the original text, the text is updated to follow that work (P-26: the type group's later word wins). The language is not redesigned. The specification is a living document that states each change that the revival makes (P-95 says how a change is recorded). A pure-Java microGPT is the baseline that compiled microGPT is measured against: the optimal result, the one to aim at.

POSITIONS.md:8

POSITIONS.md:12

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:44
- P-47 **Each integer type declares its own `MIN`, `MAX` and `MINMAX`, instead of relying on those that it inherits from the generic order traits.** The integer types are the five that `AnyIntegral` lists: `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64`. Through `Integral`, each inherits the three operators from `StandardTotalOrder` and the `StandardMin`, `StandardMax` and `StandardMinMax` that it extends. `a MINMAX b` is the pair `(a MIN b, a MAX b)`. The `MAX` that a `ZZ64` inherits types `self` as the order trait, so neither it nor `QQ`'s `MAX` is more specific. Under walk, `b MAX 1` for a `ZZ64` `b` would then stop the run with "Ambiguous coercion". With their own declarations, these operators answer at the type that their arguments promote to (P-74), as `b + 1` does. Why: it is the library's own device. `QQ`, `RR64` and the compiler's prelude declare all three, and the specification's `ZZ` declares its own `MIN` and `MAX`.

POSITIONS.md:45
- P-48 **A type parameter that a call's arguments do not fix takes its bound, never `Bottom`.** The arguments leave a parameter unfixed when it occurs only in the result type; when two arguments meet at it with no narrowest type into which both convert (a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` have one, `ZZ64`, by P-74); or when dispatch, at run time, picks a generic declaration and must choose the instance to run. Its instance is then the intersection of its upper bounds (`Any` if it has none). At checking, that is narrowed by what the call's expected type (P-49 defines it) requires of the declared return type; at run time, by the static type that the checker gave the call. It is never `Bottom`, never the union of the arguments' types, and never the value's type alone. The rule sets the instance, not which declaration runs (P-46). Why: the rule is the team's later word, from the POPL 2019 paper on multiple dispatch, and the curator trusts the team's later work above his own understanding (P-26). The rule changes nothing in microGPT, whose types are concrete. The library keeps the team's declarations of `fail`, `builtinPrimitive` and `List`'s empty comprehension, whose type parameters have no written bound, without the `extends Object` that a batch had added. Under walk, which has no static types, dispatch takes the value's type. Row 538: a compiled dispatcher that carries the static type that the checker gave the call, so that a generic declaration reached only at run time gets this instance. Rows 587, 591 and 612: three cases in which walk still gives `Bottom`.

POSITIONS.md:57
- P-60 **The specification reads a `comprises` clause at the level of values.** `trait S comprises { U, V }` says that every value of `S` is a value of `U` or of `V`. So another trait may stand between `S` and its listed types. The specification defines "covers" once: a type covers another when every value of the second is a value of the first. The Meet Rule gains a case for closed traits. Where the rule asks for a declaration at the meet of two overloads' parameter types, several declarations below both serve, if together they cover the meet. So a call whose argument's static type stands between closed traits and their listed types may have several most specific declarations. The call's type is the intersection of their return types, and the declaration that runs is unique only at run time. The compiled checker uses coverage only in its overloading rules, to accept an overload set and to justify a call's tie among several most specific declarations, and not in its general subtype test. Why: the proof addendum (`reviews/comprises-type-level-proof-addendum.md`) shows this sound for ground declarations, at calls that need no coercion. A ground declaration's types hold no type variable, and `G[\ZZ32\]` is ground. The addendum shows it for coverage used only in that way, and leaves any wider use to a review of its own. A call that needs a coercion is outside the proof too (F-76 gives what the compiled checker does there). A declaration with static parameters, whose instance dispatch must choose at run time, is outside the proof: one instance would have to meet every one of the return types at once. The typing by the intersection is not extended to it, and the specification states that boundary. Rows 543 and 551: the compiled checker gives no call an intersection type where any declaration of the family has static parameters, and walk checks no `comprises` clause declared outside the main component.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### Numbers

POSITIONS.md:73
- P-66 **The integer principle: Java's and the JVM's defaults stay where they make sense, and are corrected where they fail high performance or mathematical precision.** The team did so with rounding. A hardware behaviour that bytecode can express gets its own explicit spelling, as the specification's wrapping and saturating operators do. Where the JVM prevents a correct implementation, the project gives way for now. The peers to compare are Julia, X10, Swift and Rust.

POSITIONS.md:75
- P-68 **On the float types, `floor` and `ceiling` return the same float type, while the brackets ⌊x⌋ and ⌈x⌉, `round` and `truncate` return `ZZ`, the unbounded integer.** So `floor(2.5)` is the `RR64` value 2.0, and ⌊2.5⌋ is to be the `ZZ` value 2. Row 330: one library rung after the switch-over, which first counts the interpreter tests whose output changes, then makes the brackets, `round` and `truncate` return `ZZ` in each of the library's declarations of them; today the brackets are `ZZ64` under walk and `RR64` compiled, and `round` and `truncate` are `ZZ64`, `ZZ` or `RR64` by declaration.

POSITIONS.md:81
- P-74 **Mixed integer widths convert by declared coercions: each wider integer type declares a `coerce` from each narrower integer type, as the compiler prelude does.** A conversion that is exact is implicit, and a conversion that can lose precision is written out. So `ZZ32` values and integer numerals coerce into `RR64` implicitly, and a `ZZ64` value into `RR64` is written out (P-66, Java's defaults corrected where they lose precision). A call of a generic function with arguments of mixed widths infers, on both paths, the narrowest type into which its arguments coerce. A range is over `ZZ32` only (P-77, the rule on ranges). The specification's `widens` declaration, which would make a narrow computation stored into a wide variable run wide, is deferred. The implicit coercion of `NN32` into `RR64`: P-75 holds it, with its conflict with the overloads of `RR64` and `ZZ64`.

POSITIONS.md:82
- P-75 **`NN32` coerces into `RR64` implicitly, since every `NN32` value converts to `RR64` exactly.** Why: a conversion that fits is implicit, the rule of P-74 on mixed widths. With the coercion, an operator that both `RR64` and `ZZ64` declare is ambiguous on both paths for a `ZZ32` with an `NN32`, since neither `ZZ64` nor `RR64` coerces into the other. Without it, P-74's rule, the narrowest type into which both arguments coerce, gives `ZZ64`. Row 575: the coercion, which the tree lacks, with this conflict and its measurement. Each way to build it changes a decided behaviour, so the choice of a way is not a worker's (`fortress-repo`'s exploring part).

POSITIONS.md:83
- P-76 **An integer numeral has a type of its own, `IntLiteral`, which each number type converts from: in the interpreter's library now, and under walk once walk has the checker's static types.** The design is the compiler's prelude's working one, taken in place of the specification's numeral types, which the team left unfinished. Why the split: walk has no static types, so it would give a list of numerals the element type `IntLiteral`, with no declared type to go by. The interpreter's library declares `IntLiteral`, the conversions from it into the five integer types, `QQ` and `RR64`, and `IntLiteral`'s own arithmetic, which the team had left commented out until coercion existed. Walk still gives an integer numeral the type `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit, so no numeral reaches `IntLiteral`'s declarations under walk. Walk gaps: a numeral that walk matches as a `ZZ32` in a `typecase` or an overload (row 79), a numeral at an `NN32` or `NN64` binding (row 454), an integer numeral beyond `ZZ32`'s range at an `RR64` binding (row 443), a `nat` parameter used as a value (row 486), and coercion through tuple and varargs parameters (rows 395 and 511).

POSITIONS.md:84
- P-77 **Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only, as the compiler's prelude declares them (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`).** Why: a JVM array has at most as many elements as the largest `ZZ32`. A range over another integer type is a static error. A loop whose counter needs a wider type runs over a `ZZ32` range and widens each element, as in `j: ZZ64 = i`. A range of rank 2 or 3 is a tuple of `ZZ32` scalar ranges. The public range traits, such as `Range[\I\]`, stay generic in their index type: the ranges of rank 2 and 3 extend them at pairs and triples of `ZZ32`.

POSITIONS.md:85
- P-78 **`SUM` and `PROD` are one generic reduction each over the library's algebra, in place of the team's catch-all over `Number`, and take their identity from the static argument.** `SUM` is generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `PROD` over `MultiplicativeRing`. A reduction written with generators writes its static argument where nothing at the call fixes the element type. The compiled checker fixes it from neither the generators, the body nor a declared type that receives the value, and refuses every such `SUM` or `PROD` that leaves it out (row 731, a gap of the checker). Row 731's workaround is to write it in every clause form of `SUM` and `PROD`, as in `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. A sum without generators is written as before, with no static argument: `SUM e` over a collection `e`, and the dot product `x DOT y`. `BIG MAXN`, `BIG MINN` and `BIG MINMAXN`, the team's `Number`-typed big operators for the maximum, the minimum and both, each with an identity, are gone; no program called them. `MAX` and `MIN` get no identity on the integers or the floats, so an empty `BIG MAX` or `BIG MIN` raises `EmptyReduction` (F-60: a maximum's identity is its type's least value, which a coercion into a wider type does not carry). POSITIONS.md:87
- P-80 **The specification's sign-refined number types are a superseded design: a program tests such a subset of a type at run time.** These types are the specification's subtypes by sign, such as positive ℚ, non-negative ℚ and non-zero ℚ, and the same refinements of the integers. The machine types `NN32` and `NN64` are separate types, not among them. The specification's number chapters now test a value's sign by comparison, and a float with two getters of `RR64`: `check` returns `Just(x)` for a finite `x`, `check_star` returns `Just(x)` for an `x` that is not a NaN, and each returns `Nothing` otherwise. == explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:59
- P-146 **In a self-typed trait, the compiled checker types `self` in the method bodies as also being the implementing type.** A self-typed trait is a trait `C[\X\]` whose parameter `X` extends `C[\X\]`, such as `Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]`. In its method bodies, `self` has the type `C[\X\] & X`. The method signatures keep the plain trait type, because the proofs of the POPL 2019 paper on multiple dispatch (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu) assume that no declared type holds a type parameter inside an intersection. Only the overloading check's exclusion test reads `self` in a signature as `C[\X\] & X` (P-157). The checker refuses a type that extends such a trait at another type, since an extender must be a subtype of the static argument that it gives: `object Bad extends Integral[\ZZ32\]` is refused, because `Bad` is not a `ZZ32`. Scala has the same rule for self types. The library's text gains no self type and no `comprises` clause, and walk is unchanged. The rule accepts every self-typed method body of the library except `Integral`'s `numerator`, which each integer type declares instead. Why: the checker reads the library as the team wrote it, as P-44 does for the closure of `AnyIntegral`, by one rule that peer languages share. F-225 states the rule as built.

POSITIONS.md:60
- P-147 **An object defines an inherited abstract method when its bodies of that name at narrower parameter types together cover the abstract method's parameter types.** That is, each value of the abstract method's parameter types is a value of one body's parameter types. A `comprises` clause counts as the compiled checker reads it, which is P-60's reading: a closed trait is covered by its listed types. A body at the abstract method's own parameter types is the plain case. This is the team's rule of 2012, in Steele's abstract-method check of the compiled checker and in the Covered rule of the Welterweight calculus (`Papers/Welterweight/`). So the team's `Library/Pairs.fss` and `ProjectFortress/tests/FileConversion.fss` stay valid: an object in each defines an inherited abstract operator once for each type that a `comprises` clause lists. Walk applies the same rule at load, and its earlier allowance of any one narrower body goes. The traits chapter's sentence, which admitted no narrower body, is revised in the specification's revision form (P-96). Row 725: the acceptance of some valid objects whose methods have static parameters of their own, which the checker and walk (row 728) refuse. Row 665: walk's check of generic objects, which its load check skips.

POSITIONS.md:62
- P-149 **An object that inherits an abstract functional method from one trait, and a body for it from a sibling trait, is refused unless it declares the method itself.** In `object O extends { A, B }`, where `A` declares `pick(self)` abstract and `B` gives `pick(self)` a body, `O` must declare its own `pick`. Scala's way, where the sibling trait's body implements the abstract method, is not taken. The compiled checker refuses such an object, as the specification's text and the type group's Welterweight calculus (`Papers/Welterweight/`) require. Walk already refuses it at load, by the Meet Rule for Functional Methods. A trait that declares one method both abstract and with a body, at the same parameter types, is refused too. Why: the revival honors the designers' intent. It changes Fortress's nature only to reconcile a conflict between the earlier and the later designers' choices, and then looks to other languages for how to do it. Here there is no such conflict, and Fortress is not bent to Scala's way for a hypothetical convenience.

POSITIONS.md:64
- P-152 **Walk and the compiled checker read the exclusion of two generic declarations over their whole parameter types, by existential reduction.** With static parameters, the parameter types of two declarations can exclude each other as a whole, even where no single parameter excludes its counterpart. In `o[\T\](x: P[\T\], b: Box[\T\])` beside `o[\T\](x: Q[\T\], b: Box[\T\])`, where `P[\T\]` excludes `Q[\T\]` only at the same `T`, neither parameter excludes alone. But no value is a `Box` of two types, so `b` fixes the same `T` for both declarations, and no argument fits both. A generic trait in `Box`'s place fixes `T` in the same way. Both paths read such a pair as excluding, and judge it on that reading by the overloading rules (P-45: the 2011 paper's No Duplicates, Meet and Return Type rules). Why: the type group's 2011 paper decides exclusion between parameter types with static parameters by existential reduction (`Papers/Types/exc-reduction.tick`; P-26, the type group's later word outweighs the specification's early text), as the revised specification states (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`, "Declarations with Static Parameters"). Walk refuses such a pair at load where one declaration has a `where` clause, which the checker accepts (row 787); and walk reads an object type over a static parameter, such as `Box[\T\]`, as excluding a type that it equals at some instance, such as `Box[\ZZ32\]`, so that it loads a pair that the checker refuses (row 788).

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### Numbers

POSITIONS.md:88
- P-153 **The integer power splits on the base: an integer base gives an integer or raises an error, and a float or rational base gives the fraction.** Each integer type's `^` returns its own type at every exponent. At a negative exponent, the bases 1 and -1 give their exact power, a base of 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and any other base raises `IntegerOverflow`. A program that wants a fraction writes a float or rational base, as in `2.0^(-1)`. Why: the team's later code gives an integer power the type of its integer base at a signed exponent (P-26, the team's later work outweighs the specification's early text). Overloads choose by type, and no type tells a negative exponent from a non-negative one, since a signed integer or a numeral can be either. So the split is on the base, and the sign of the exponent is tested at run time, as the library tests a value's sign everywhere (P-80, run-time sign tests in place of sign-refined types). Row 441: the same rule on the compiled path, whose own powers give 0 at a negative exponent and a raw Java exception at a base of 0, and overflow silently or with a raw Java exception (row 523).

POSITIONS.md:65
- P-154 **A list is ordered only where its element type is totally ordered.** The library's `List` extends its lexicographic order only where its element type extends `StandardTotalOrder` (conditional extension, P-151). Floats and `QQ` are only partially ordered, since NaN, and `QQ`'s 0/0, compare with nothing. So on the compiled checker a list of floats or of `QQ` has no order: no `<`, `CMP` or the other comparisons, though its `=` stays. A pair of floats stays ordered: the curator accepted that mismatch as a cost of the list rule. The tuples' own rule is not decided here. No lexicographic trait over partially ordered elements is added now: the team never wrote one, and the case touches neither the distance to the switch-over nor microGPT. Why: the team's later code bounds the element of both of its lexicographic traits by a total order (`Library/incomplete/advanced/Fortress.PartialTotalOrders.fss:117-140`; P-26, the team's later word outweighs its early text), and conditional extension is a `where` form that the team wrote (P-151). Row 774: walk's half, since walk still gives every list an order.

POSITIONS.md:66
- P-155 **The compiled checker checks the overloads of symbolic operators before the switch-over.** Today its overloading check reads an operator only if its name is a word of capitals, such as `MAX`, so `+`, `^`, `||`, the subscripts and the other symbolic operators pass unchecked. The check must read them by the rules that it applies to any function, so that the distance to the switch-over reaches zero with them checked. Why: the skip is a gap that the team knew, not a rule: the specification's appendix of proposed features calls the library's two subscript operators "not really a valid overloading" (`Specification/appendices/future.tex:186-207`, its item on array indexing). A zero with them unchecked would hide known errors. Each design that the check needs is brought to the curator before its rung, with the probe's measurement (`perf-probes/symbolic-operators-2/REPORT.md`); the two it found are decided: P-156, the subscripts' index bound, and P-157, vectors that stay additive groups by a change to the checker's exclusion test. Row 584: the check and its rungs.

POSITIONS.md:67
- P-156 **A collection's index type extends `Index`, a trait that the ranges exclude, and a tuple of indices is an `Index`.** Every index parameter of the library's generic indexed types is bounded `I extends Index`; `ZZ32` extends `Index`, and `Range` excludes it. So a subscript that takes one index and a subscript that takes a range never apply to the same value, and the pair is a valid overloading at every instance. - F-282 **The compiled export check matches an api's members by name and header and reads `abstract`, and the `FortressLibrary` component matches its api.** It matches an api member with a component member of the same name and header, and a field by its name, its modifiers other than `var` and its type. It compares the component's abstract members against the api's, and asks no definition for an api member written `abstract` (`Specification/basic/components/apis.tex:252-256`). So a component may leave out, or declare at another header, a member its api writes `abstract`, and a client's call of it dies at run time with `NoSuchMethodError` (row 816). `FortressLibrary.fsi` states its component's members at the component's headers. It leaves out the subscripts the component never built (`Just`'s and `Nothing`'s 1.0 range subscripts, the arrays' `OpenRange` subscripts). Where the api's type is the contract, the component takes it: `RR64`'s brackets and `truncate` at `ZZ64`, `DelegatedIndexed`'s `generator`, and `Array2`'s and `Array3`'s `bounds` and `zeroIndices`. `String`'s api writes `abstract` on the members its component's trait leaves without a body or does not declare, and its `excludes` clause is the component's (F-286). <!-- This file lists, for each POSITIONS entry that the reports of the foundations review name, what the reports found about the entry's text, with the exact source and where the record already holds it; a retrieval worker wrote it on 2026-10-27, and it judges nothing. -->

# The foundations review, entry by entry

"At issue" quotes POSITIONS.md as it stands (last changed at 5da8144e4, 2026-10-26). In "Reports", [..] replaces the reports' layer shorthand and "…" a cut. Sources, in explorations/reviews/foundations/: judgement.md, tenets-evidence.md ("evidence map"), prelude-lens.md ("prelude sweep"), bound-archaeology.md ("bound report"), rewrite-results.md ("rewrite note"), evidence/trap-test/key.md and grades.md; "dialogue" is conversations/02-phase3-exit-foundations.md. 0d2206c5f is the routing commit of 2026-10-26 08:56 UTC: rows 832, 833, 339, 412, 470, 691; F-9, F-18, F-44, F-84, F-225, F-289, F-291, F-292; review-queue item 278. "Old reader": the trap-test reader with today's entries (10 of 12).

**P-7**, how later work revises the text.
At issue: "the team's later work, in the compiler or in the papers on types"
Reports: "'Later work in the compiler' is two things: a rule the team's checker enforces on purpose … and an accommodation of the JVM or of a checker gap …. P-7 should not restate the rule; it should point to P-26" (judgement §2, tenet 1).
Plain: Layers mixed: a deliberate rule and a JVM workaround are not told apart.
Ground: the judge's reasoning only. The sentence follows the curator's words of 2026-10-12 23:15:30 UTC.
Elsewhere: no.

**P-8**, deciding by the goal where sources are silent. No fault found. (Judgement §2, tenet 1: right if an implementation's word is read as JVM evidence.)

**P-12**, walk runs the checker after the switch-over.
At issue: "After it, walk runs the checker on its programs and so gains their static types."
Reports: "walk has no case for `CoercionInvocation` (…); walk would then take the checker's own departures (rows 470, 731) as its own; and F-290's 624 errors stand between the checker and the components walk's programs import" (judgement §2, tenet 9).
Plain: The step is bigger than the entry says: the Scala checker switched on under walk, walk reading the inserted coercions, the imported components cleared. Unmeasured.
Ground: code reading (`Shell.java:420-424`, `StaticChecker.java:228-229`) and F-290; nothing run. The "small change" told to the curator on 2026-09-29 14:08:16 UTC was the coordinator's.
Elsewhere: facts in F-9 and row 833 (0d2206c5f); the entry: no. Naming rows 470 and 731 is a queue item of the rewrite note, "Still owed".

**P-17**, unboxed doubles are required.
At issue: "Why: a language meant for high performance cannot box its numbers."
Reports: "they do not cite `objects.tex:38` or `binary.tex:76-82`, which are the [language] grounds that answer "is unboxing the language's intent or only ours"" (judgement §2, tenet 7).
Plain: Missing reason: the specification's own words, value objects "an implementation may freely copy" and a `LinearSequence` of a value type "describes a sequence of 'unboxed' values".
Ground: Working Draft `basic/objects.tex:38`, `advanced-lib/binary.tex:80`; the judge's reasoning. The Why is the curator's (2026-09-19 18:32:48 UTC).
Elsewhere: no (F-11 holds the measurement only).

**P-25**, the 2012 Types chapter beside the specification. Named as a link of P-7 and P-26. No fault found.

**P-26** (a), why the later word wins.
At issue: "worked to make the language run, with performance as the goal and specialization a must, and learned what is feasible"
Reports: "A JVM limit the team hit is evidence about [the JVM layer], not a reason to rank a [language] text" (judgement §2, tenet 2).
Plain: Wrong layer.
Ground: the judge's reasoning, on the curator's three-layers frame (2026-10-26 05:25:27 UTC). The sentence follows his words of 2026-09-23 07:26:28 UTC. The old reader was not misled (trap grades §4).
Elsewhere: no.

**P-26** (b), the list of the later word.
At issue: "the number types of the compiler's prelude made siblings in 2009 and 2010"; "specialization kept"
Reports: "is [JVM-layer] code, earlier than the [Working Draft's] last edit (2010-12), earlier than the 2011 paper, with no stated reason" (judgement §2, tenet 2).
Plain: Wrong layer and date. "Specialization" is an overload chosen at run time here, a class per instantiation in the skill's `exploring.md`.
Ground: commit 6896886fb (Chase, 2009-08-31); its message ends "this would be a good time to get coercion working". Working Draft last edited 2010-12-09.
Elsewhere: no.

**P-26** (c), a sentence with no source.
At issue: "The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text."
Reports: "…is the coordinator's sentence with no source (review-queue item 215)" (judgement §2, tenet 2); its §9 item 4 says strike it.
Plain: Reason not the curator's. Nothing rests on it.
Ground: commit bc8902f47 (2026-09-30) added it; no message of his says it (positions audit, note on P-26, §3).
Elsewhere: review-queue item 215, open.

**P-26** (d), no test for "later".
At issue: "The revival does not second-guess them: it knows less than they did."
Reports: "(4) date a code commit against the texts before calling it "later"; (5) where two later sources conflict, stop ranking and decide by P-8's goal, saying so" (judgement §7).
Plain: Missing rule: how to date "later", and what to do when two later sources conflict. The old reader decided worse in scenario 2 (1 of 2) for want of it.
Ground: the judge's reasoning; trap grades §4; evidence map, "What I could not find" 4. He said yes to rewording P-26 and P-37 at 2026-10-26 07:42:15 UTC.
Elsewhere: no.

**P-27**, the library's practice is the standard.
At issue: "The library's own practice is the standard."
Reports: "supplied Y's wrong-[layer] ground … P-27 governs how the library is extended … It does not decide between two of the team's own designs; the dated later word does" (trap grades §4; Y is the old reader).
Plain: Read alone, it led the old reader to drop a rung because "the library never had the clause".
Ground: trap test, scenario 2; the grader's reasoning.
Elsewhere: no (review-queue items 216 and 237 hold P-27 for other questions).

**P-33**, the phase order.
At issue: "reports no error on the interpreter's whole library"
Reports: ""The interpreter's whole library" is wider than F-53's twelve, and his 10-26 goal says "the fuller library". No step names the bound flip (F-289)." (judgement §2, tenet 6).
Plain: False in scope: the zero covers twelve components (fourteen with `List`'s two imports). The other 38 block P-12's step, not the switch-over. No step flips the bound. The code-generator half was unmeasured at approval (52 refusals, F-34).
Ground: F-53, F-290, F-289, F-34; the curator's words of 2026-10-24 11:36:23 and 2026-10-26 04:47:50 and 07:30:36 UTC; fourteen and 38: dialogue §9.
Elsewhere: those FACTS; BOOT.md ask 3. The entry: no.

**P-37** (a), the reason is missing.
At issue: "as a bootstrap to remove"
Reports: "His goal of 10-26 ("avoid the need to port walk's library into the compiler's library; continue the type checker so that it accepts the fuller library") is the [language] reason and is not in the entry" (judgement §2, tenet 3).
Plain: Missing reason of the curator's. Without it the old reader listed a `CompilerSystem` bridge as an option (scenario 4: 1 of 2).
Ground: his words, 2026-10-26 04:47:50 UTC: "The whole point of the switchover is to avoid the need to port walks library into the compilers library. Revival is continuing the development of type checker, so that it would accept the fuller Fortress library that the interpreter uses."
Elsewhere: dialogue §4 only.

**P-37** (b), a permission with no rule.
At issue: "the one library may take a design of the prelude's, as it took the prelude's flat shape of the number types"
Reports: "this reads an [JVM-layer] bootstrap as a design source with no rule for when" (judgement §2, tenet 3).
Plain: Missing rule. The judge's rule (§3): a prelude design binds if the team's later language text backs it, or the text is unclear and the team's checker enforced it. A stub or a workaround does not. "Later" is a date. The old reader kept way 5 open for want of it (scenario 2: 1 of 2).
Ground: the judge's reasoning, on the curator's caution (2026-10-26 07:30:36; "Yes. Exactly." 07:36:39 UTC).
Elsewhere: two designs found not to bind are in F-84 and F-225 (0d2206c5f); the rule: no.

**P-37** (c), the premise.
At issue: "the compiled path reads the interpreter's library with it"
Reports: "So the premise is unmeasured, not refuted. … F-34 and [the phase 3 exit judgement's] two phase-4 zeros are now the answer, and the entry should carry it" (judgement §2, tenet 3).
Plain: Missing: the library has been shown to check, not to run, compiled. Two zeros stand between (checker, code generator).
Ground: F-34 (52 refusals); rows 339 and 832; the curator's doubt of 2026-09-20 15:18:35 UTC.
Elsewhere: F-34, F-291, rows 339 and 832 (0d2206c5f); the entry: no.

**P-37** (d), three files.
At issue: "its own library files `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra`"
Reports: "names three files, so that `CompilerSystem` falls outside its letter" (trap key, scenario 4).
Plain: The prelude has a fourth wired file, `CompilerSystem`, that 27 compiled tests import.
Ground: prelude sweep §0 (four files); `reviews/phase3-exit/zero-audit.md`, A.2.
Elsewhere: no.

**P-38**, the prelude's defects go with it. Named as P-37's cross-reference. No fault found.

**P-42** (a), "functions".
At issue: "`Any` holds tuples, functions and `()`, which `Object` does not."
Reports: ""Functions" (review-queue item 218): the [Working Draft] puts arrows outside `Object`, the Types chapter inside; drop the word, as the specification's callout already does" (judgement §4).
Plain: The team's texts disagree on functions and agree on tuples and `()`. His yes rested on the tuples.
Ground: Working Draft `types-vals-vars.tex:136`, `:215-216` against `types.tick:232-238`; his yes 2026-09-29 14:02:25 UTC, after the coordinator's wrong text of 13:58:02.
Elsewhere: review-queue item 218, open.

**P-42** (b), the departure.
At issue: "which ends the departure"
Reports: "the switch-over ends nothing by itself; `Shell.java:372` does, and no step named it (F-289, 685 errors under the command's setting)" (judgement §4).
Plain: False. One line of `Shell.java` holds `Object`. No plan step flips it. `()` and a tuple-typed dotted method fail under either bound.
Ground: `Shell.java:371-386`; Steele's 91e71e62e, c61723f61, afb02f41d (2012-05-28 to 30); F-289, F-291.
Elsewhere: F-289, F-291, rows 412, 339, 832 (0d2206c5f); the flip is rung B of climb batch 22c.

**P-42** (c), grounds missing.
At issue: "The specification states the bound `Any`, with a callout"
Reports: "(1) cite POPL 2019, the [Working Draft's] instantiation sentence and the library's practice as the grounds" (judgement §7).
Plain: Missing: POPL 2019 ("By default, each type parameter has an upper bound Any"); the Working Draft's own line that parameters take tuple and arrow types; Steele's 2012 setting enforced one sentence on one path.
Ground: `research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019.txt:418-419`; `trait-parameters.tex:53-54`; bound report §1, §2.6.
Elsewhere: no.

**P-42** (d), a stale example.
At issue: "its arrays indexed by pairs, such as `(ZZ32,ZZ32)`, are among them"
Reports: "Since P-156, the arrays' index parameter has an explicit bound `Index`, so P-42's example "arrays indexed by pairs" no longer rests on the implicit bound; element types such as `(E,F)` still do" (evidence map, tenet 4(c)).
Plain: False as an example.
Ground: P-156's text; `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:759`, `:1364`.
Elsewhere: no.

**P-43** (a), the reason is not his.
At issue: "Why: the flattened prelude is the team's last record of the Fortress way, and its route leads to the POPL 2019 paper, which keeps the rule."
Reports: "…misdated: "the flattened prelude is the team's last record of the Fortress way" (2009 code, earlier than every text above; his phrase "the team's last record" was about the forest rule, rq 219)" (judgement §2, tenet 5).
Plain: Reason not his, wrong layer and date. The POPL 2019 paper keeps the rule but has no numbers and no tower.
Ground: his words 2026-09-24 01:02:52 UTC (of the patents' forest rule) and 14:41:40 ("Agreed. Route A it is.", no reason); commit 6896886fb. He said on 2026-10-26 07:46:17 UTC: "I think we did a plenty of digging which decided why we took the flat numeric tower."
Elsewhere: review-queue item 219, open.

**P-43** (b), specialisation.
At issue: "He cares that specialised code runs fast, not how a specialisation is chosen."
Reports: "…joins the two meanings of specialisation and he said it was not an answer (rq 220)" (judgement §2, tenet 5).
Plain: Reason not clearly his: in the same message (2026-09-24 01:02:52 UTC) he wrote "Which clearly isn't an answer to the question".
Ground: his words; the coordinator's account of the two meanings (01:05:02 UTC).
Elsewhere: review-queue item 220, open.

**P-43** (c), the language's grounds are missing.
At issue: "The compiled checker keeps the multiple instantiation exclusion rule."
Reports: "The exclusion rule is the type group's published position four times over … The [Working Draft's] own types chapter says the numeric types "are mutually exclusive; no value has more than one of them" (`types-vals-vars.tex:502`)" (judgement §2, tenet 5).
Plain: Missing: the 2011 paper (`exclusion.tick:141-152`), the 2012 Types chapter (`types.tick:355-376`), Naden 2012 (`justificationOfRTR.tex:496-497`), POPL 2019, that sentence; and the prelude's flat shape as the compiled world's instance of the same answer.
Ground: those lines.
Elsewhere: F-44 (JVM type mapping, `TypeMapping.tex:125`, added in 0d2206c5f) and F-46; the sentence is in no FACTS or POSITIONS entry.

**P-44**, `AnyIntegral` stays closed. Named as a use of the 2012 texts as the later word, and in P-146's reason. No fault found.

**P-47**, each integer type's own `MIN`, `MAX`, `MINMAX`. Named as rightly taken from the prelude (judgement §3). No fault found.

**P-48**, an unfixed type parameter takes its bound. Named: the judgement finds it is POPL 2019's own rule (§3). No fault found.

**P-58** (a), the reason.
At issue: "the library's own form, and it keeps that form"
Reports: "The entry's ground "the specification prints `builtinPrimitive`'s declaration" is weak: it is true only through the included library api, whose comment describes walk's mechanism. The sound ground is the layer and the practice." (judgement §2, tenet 8).
Plain: Weak reason, in the entry's first text (2026-10-10, 046207371). The present text gives none. The form is outside the language, so the library's practice (all 424 bindings) decides.
Ground: Working Draft `appendices/future.tex:675` (no foreign-function interface); `FortressBuiltin.fsi:14-29`; F-32; the judge's reasoning.
Elsewhere: no.

**P-58** (b), his informed yes.
At issue: the decision as a whole.
Reports: "the yes must be informed and must come before climb batch 23, since after 449 bindings move the other form costs a library sweep" (judgement §2, tenet 8).
Plain: Owed. On 2026-10-22 22:02:17 UTC he wrote: "I don't recall my decision asking for static methods so I am unable to make fully informed decision from this fragment." None found to 2026-10-26 07:00 UTC.
Ground: his words.
Elsewhere: BOOT.md ask 4; `reviews/phase3-exit/judgement.md` §1 item 5.

**P-59**, walk's coercions.
At issue: "MicroGPT's static types are concrete, each the type of the value itself and not a trait above it, so on microGPT walk's choice and the static choice agree."
Reports: "P-59's "microGPT's static types are concrete" is the coordinator's premise, unmeasured (rq 221), measurable only when microGPT compiles" (judgement §2, tenet 9).
Plain: Reason not the curator's; unmeasured.

<!-- This file lists, for each POSITIONS entry that the reports of the foundations review name, what the reports found about the entry's text, with the exact source and where the record already holds it; a retrieval worker wrote it on 2026-10-27, and it judges nothing. -->

# The foundations review, entry by entry

"At issue" quotes POSITIONS.md as it stands (last changed 5da8144e4, 2026-10-26). In quotes, [..] replaces a layer shorthand and "…" a cut. Sources, in explorations/reviews/foundations/: judgement.md, tenets-evidence.md (evidence map), prelude-lens.md (prelude sweep), bound-archaeology.md (bound report), rewrite-results.md (rewrite note), evidence/trap-test/key.md and grades.md; "dialogue" is conversations/02-phase3-exit-foundations.md. 0d2206c5f is the routing commit of 2026-10-26 08:56 UTC (rows 832, 833, 339, 412, 470, 691; F-9, F-18, F-44, F-84, F-225, F-289, F-291, F-292; review-queue item 278). Old reader: the trap-test reader with today's entries (10 of 12).

**P-7**, how later work revises the text.
At issue: "the team's later work, in the compiler or in the papers on types"
Reports: "'Later work in the compiler' is two things: a rule the team's checker enforces on purpose … and an accommodation of the JVM or of a checker gap" (judgement §2, tenet 1).
Plain: Layers mixed. It should point to P-26 and not restate the rule.
Ground: the judge's reasoning only. Elsewhere: no.

**P-8**, deciding by the goal. No fault found (judgement §2, tenet 1 only adds: read an implementation's word as JVM evidence).

**P-12**, walk runs the checker after the switch-over.
At issue: "After it, walk runs the checker on its programs and so gains their static types."
Reports: "walk has no case for `CoercionInvocation` …; and F-290's 624 errors stand between the checker and the components walk's programs import" (judgement §2, tenet 9).
Plain: Bigger than the entry says: the Scala checker on under walk, walk reading inserted coercions, imported components cleared. Unmeasured.
Ground: code reading (`StaticChecker.java:228-229`) and F-290; nothing run. Elsewhere: F-9 and row 833 (0d2206c5f); the entry: no.

**P-17**, unboxed doubles are required.
At issue: "Why: a language meant for high performance cannot box its numbers."
Reports: "they do not cite `objects.tex:38` or `binary.tex:76-82`, which are the [language] grounds that answer "is unboxing the language's intent or only ours"" (judgement §2, tenet 7).
Plain: Missing reason: value objects "an implementation may freely copy"; a `LinearSequence` of a value type "describes a sequence of 'unboxed' values".
Ground: Working Draft `objects.tex:38`, `binary.tex:80`; the judge's reasoning. Elsewhere: no (F-11 is the measurement only).

**P-25**, the 2012 Types chapter cited beside the specification. A link of P-7 and P-26 only. No fault found.

**P-26** (a), the reason and the list.
At issue: "learned what is feasible"; "the number types of the compiler's prelude made siblings in 2009 and 2010"
Reports: "A JVM limit the team hit is evidence about [the JVM layer], not a reason to rank a [language] text"; the flat numbers are "[JVM-layer] code, earlier than the [Working Draft's] last edit (2010-12), earlier than the 2011 paper, with no stated reason" (judgement §2, tenet 2).
Plain: Wrong layer, and a 2009 date counted as "later".
Ground: the judge's reasoning on his three-layers frame (2026-10-26 05:25:27 UTC); commit 6896886fb (Chase, 2009-08-31). The old reader was not misled (trap grades §4). Elsewhere: no.

**P-26** (b), a sentence with no source.
At issue: "The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text."
Reports: "…is the coordinator's sentence with no source (review-queue item 215)" (judgement §2, tenet 2); strike it (§9, item 4).
Plain: Reason not the curator's. Nothing rests on it.
Ground: commit bc8902f47 (2026-09-30) added it; no message of his says it (positions audit, P-26 note §3). Elsewhere: review-queue item 215, open.

**P-26** (c), no test for "later".
At issue: "The revival does not second-guess them: it knows less than they did."
Reports: "(4) date a code commit against the texts before calling it "later"; (5) where two later sources conflict, stop ranking and decide by P-8's goal, saying so" (judgement §7).
Plain: Missing rule for "later", for code commits and for two conflicting later sources; also one word for each of the two "specialisations". The old reader decided worse in scenario 2 (1 of 2).
Ground: the judge's reasoning; trap grades §4. He said yes to rewording P-26 and P-37 at 2026-10-26 07:42:15 UTC. Elsewhere: no.

**P-27**, the library's practice is the standard.
At issue: "The library's own practice is the standard."
Reports: "supplied Y's wrong-[layer] ground … P-27 governs how the library is extended … It does not decide between two of the team's own designs; the dated later word does" (trap grades §4; Y is the old reader).
Plain: Read alone, it led the old reader to drop a rung because "the interpreter's library never had a clause on these traits".
Ground: trap test, scenario 2; the grader's reasoning. Elsewhere: no.

**P-33**, the phase order.
At issue: "reports no error on the interpreter's whole library"
Reports: ""The interpreter's whole library" is wider than F-53's twelve, and his 10-26 goal says "the fuller library". No step names the bound flip (F-289)." (judgement §2, tenet 6).
Plain: The zero covers twelve components (fourteen with `List`'s two imports). The other 38 block P-12's step, not the switch-over. The code-generator half was unmeasured at approval (52 refusals, F-34).
Ground: F-53, F-290, F-289, F-34; his words of 2026-10-24 11:36:23 and 2026-10-26 04:47:50 and 07:30:36 UTC; fourteen and 38: dialogue §9. Elsewhere: those FACTS; BOOT.md ask 3; the entry: no.

**P-37** (a), his reason is missing.
At issue: "as a bootstrap to remove"
Reports: "His goal of 10-26 ("avoid the need to port walk's library into the compiler's library; continue the type checker so that it accepts the fuller library") is the [language] reason and is not in the entry" (judgement §2, tenet 3).
Plain: Without it the old reader listed a `CompilerSystem` bridge as an option (scenario 4: 1 of 2).
Ground: his words, 2026-10-26 04:47:50 UTC: "The whole point of the switchover is to avoid the need to port walks library into the compilers library." Elsewhere: dialogue §4 only.

**P-37** (b), a permission with no rule.
At issue: "the one library may take a design of the prelude's, as it took the prelude's flat shape of the number types"
Reports: "this reads an [JVM-layer] bootstrap as a design source with no rule for when" (judgement §2, tenet 3).
Plain: Missing rule (judgement §3): a prelude design binds if the team's later language text backs it, or the text is unclear and the team's checker enforced it; a stub or workaround never; "later" is a date. Old reader: scenario 2, 1 of 2.
Ground: the judge's reasoning, on his caution (2026-10-26 07:30:36; "Yes. Exactly." 07:36:39 UTC). Elsewhere: two designs that do not bind are in F-84 and F-225 (0d2206c5f); the rule: no.

**P-37** (c), the premise.
At issue: "the compiled path reads the interpreter's library with it"
Reports: "So the premise is unmeasured, not refuted. … F-34 and [the phase 3 exit judgement's] two phase-4 zeros are now the answer, and the entry should carry it" (judgement §2, tenet 3).
Plain: The library has been shown to check, not to run, compiled. Two zeros stand between: checker and code generator.
Ground: F-34 (52 refusals), rows 339 and 832; his doubt of 2026-09-20 15:18:35 UTC. Elsewhere: F-34, F-291, those rows (0d2206c5f); the entry: no.

**P-37** (d), three files.
At issue: "its own library files `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra`"
Reports: "names three files, so that `CompilerSystem` falls outside its letter" (trap key, scenario 4).
Plain: A fourth wired file, `CompilerSystem`, is imported by 27 compiled tests.
Ground: prelude sweep §0; `reviews/phase3-exit/zero-audit.md` A.2. Elsewhere: no.

**P-38**, the prelude's defects go with it. A cross-reference of P-37 only. No fault found.

**P-42** (a), "functions".
At issue: "`Any` holds tuples, functions and `()`, which `Object` does not."
Reports: ""Functions" (review-queue item 218): the [Working Draft] puts arrows outside `Object`, the Types chapter inside; drop the word, as the specification's callout already does" (judgement §4).
Plain: The team's texts disagree on functions and agree on tuples and `()`. His yes rested on the tuples.
Ground: `types-vals-vars.tex:136`, `:215-216` against `types.tick:232-238`; his yes 2026-09-29 14:02:25 UTC after the coordinator's wrong text of 13:58:02. Elsewhere: review-queue item 218, open.

**P-42** (b), the departure.
At issue: "which ends the departure"
Reports: "the switch-over ends nothing by itself; `Shell.java:372` does, and no step named it (F-289, 685 errors under the command's setting)" (judgement §4).
Plain: False: one line of `Shell.java` holds `Object`, and no plan step flips it. `()` and a tuple-typed dotted method fail under either bound.
Ground: `Shell.java:371-386`; Steele's 91e71e62e, c61723f61, afb02f41d (2012-05-28 to 30); F-289. Elsewhere: F-289, F-291, rows 412, 339, 832 (0d2206c5f); the flip is rung B of climb batch 22c.

**P-42** (c), grounds missing.
At issue: "The specification states the bound `Any`, with a callout"
Reports: "(1) cite POPL 2019, the [Working Draft's] instantiation sentence and the library's practice as the grounds" (judgement §7).
Plain: POPL 2019 says "By default, each type parameter has an upper bound Any". The Working Draft itself says parameters take tuple and arrow types. Steele's 2012 setting enforced one sentence on one path.
Ground: `research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019.txt:418-419`; `trait-parameters.tex:53-54`; bound report §1, §2.6. Elsewhere: no.

**P-42** (d), a stale example.
At issue: "its arrays indexed by pairs, such as `(ZZ32,ZZ32)`, are among them"
Reports: "Since P-156, the arrays' index parameter has an explicit bound `Index`, so P-42's example "arrays indexed by pairs" no longer rests on the implicit bound" (evidence map, tenet 4(c)).
Plain: False as an example; element types such as `(E,F)` still rest on it.
Ground: P-156's text; `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:759`, `:1364`. Elsewhere: no.

**P-43** (a), two reasons not his.
At issue: "the flattened prelude is the team's last record of the Fortress way"; "He cares that specialised code runs fast, not how a specialisation is chosen."
Reports: "…misdated: "the flattened prelude is the team's last record of the Fortress way" (2009 code, earlier than every text above; his phrase "the team's last record" was about the forest rule, rq 219)"; the second "joins the two meanings of specialisation and he said it was not an answer (rq 220)" (judgement §2, tenet 5).
Plain: Reasons not his; wrong layer and date. The POPL 2019 paper keeps the rule but has no numbers and no tower.
Ground: his words 2026-09-24 01:02:52 UTC (of the patents' forest rule; also "Which clearly isn't an answer to the question") and 14:41:40 ("Agreed. Route A it is.", no reason); commit 6896886fb. Elsewhere: review-queue items 219 and 220, open.
